aboard.title: Before you leave
aboard.outcome: Use boat terminology, identify essential equipment, and prepare a safe crew briefing.

wind.title: Your first sail
wind.outcome: Read the wind, raise sails, get underway, and hold a steady course.

trim.title: Make the wind work
trim.outcome: Recognize points of sail and connect sail angle with speed and heading.

maneuvers.title: Change direction
maneuvers.outcome: Head up, bear away, tack, gybe, and recover from the no-go zone.

conditions.title: Stay in control
conditions.outcome: Distinguish true and apparent wind, reduce sail, and make conservative weather decisions.

navigation.title: Find your way
navigation.outcome: Interpret a practice chart, steer a bearing, monitor depth, and execute a short route.

seamanship.title: Share the water
seamanship.outcome: Maintain a lookout and reason through basic traffic and weather situations.

harbor.title: Arrive and depart
harbor.outcome: Plan docking and anchoring, rehearse stopping, and prepare for departure.

readiness.title: Respond and review
readiness.outcome: Explain emergency priorities and demonstrate a complete simulated sailing exercise.

coastal-decisions.title: Coastal decisions
coastal-decisions.outcome: Plan conservative coastal passages, calculate simple margins, and cross-check navigation information.

sail-01.title: Safety before speed
concepts: A good departure begins with the crew, weather, and boat, not the throttle. Wear a correctly fitted lifejacket, identify emergency equipment, and agree how to call for help and recover a person from the water.

Brief everyone on the boom, trip hazards, safe handholds, and keeping hands clear of loaded lines and winches. Check the forecast, local restrictions, communications, fuel or battery supply, and that the boat is seaworthy.

Choose conditions appropriate to the least experienced crew member and agree an abort plan. This course develops understanding and selected simulated skills; completion is not a qualification to skipper a real yacht.
observe: Before departure, tell your crew where to sit, how to move, and who will keep lookout.
Identify the boom and imagine its sweep across the cockpit.
sail-01.mistake: Starting because the weather looks pleasant without checking the forecast or briefing the crew.

quiz.prompt: A new crew member is aboard. What comes before departure?
options: Fit lifejackets and explain hazards, emergency equipment, and roles
Leave first and explain the controls underway
quiz.explanation: Prepare the crew and boat before getting underway; discovering a missing safety item after departure is too late.

quiz.prompt: What does passing this simulator course establish?
options: Understanding and selected skills in a simplified simulation
Readiness to sail alone in all weather
quiz.explanation: On-water instruction and assessment are still needed. The simulator omits many physical and environmental demands.

sail-01.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-02.title: Know your yacht
concepts: Bow means the front; stern means the back. Port is the left side and starboard the right when facing the bow. These names stay with the boat when you turn around.
The mainsail is behind the mast; the headsail is forward. The boom supports the mainsail foot. The keel contributes stability and resists sideways motion; the rudder steers when water flows over it.
Use Chase for the whole boat, Helm for the sailing viewpoint, and Cockpit to inspect the wheel, winches, and screens.
observe: Switch to Cockpit and locate the wheel, companionway, and sheet winches.
Switch to Chase and identify the bow, mast, boom, and two sails.
sail-02.mistake: Calling a side port or starboard from whichever direction you happen to be looking.

quiz.prompt: You are facing the stern. Which side is port?
options: Whichever side the wind comes from
quiz.explanation: Port is the yacht’s left when facing forward, so it is on your right when facing aft.

quiz.prompt: What needs water flowing over it to steer effectively?
quiz.explanation: The rudder changes the direction of water flow. With little boat speed its authority is reduced.

sail-02.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-03.title: Lines, winches, and loads
concepts: A halyard raises a sail. A sheet adjusts its angle. A reef reduces exposed sail area. A cleat or clutch holds a line; a winch helps manage load.

On this yacht, colored sheets run aft toward the cockpit winches. Inspect the wraps and clutches in Cockpit view. The Boat systems panel controls the two halyards and sheets independently, plus traveler, vang, outhaul, reefs, engine, and anchor rode. The sliders represent control settings, not physical line handling.

The main and headsail hoists set how much sail is exposed. The two sheets change sail angle independently. The traveler moves the boom’s sheeting position; vang tension controls modeled twist, while the outhaul flattens the modeled sail foot. Change one control at a time and compare the response.

Reef level reduces mainsail area. Engine throttle selects reverse, neutral, or ahead; return to neutral for sailing assessments. The anchor rode slider sets a target. Run the windlass to pay out or retrieve line over time; watch actual paid-out rode and stop the windlass when needed.
Keep fingers, loose clothing, and hair clear of loaded lines. Learn real winch loading, line handling, knots, and controlled easing with an instructor; a mouse cannot teach the feel of a loaded line.
observe: Follow a colored sheet from the deck toward its winch.
Compare a halyard’s lifting purpose with a sheet’s trimming purpose.
sail-03.mistake: Treating a heavily loaded sheet like an unloaded rope, or confusing the sheet with the halyard.

quiz.prompt: You want to adjust the mainsail’s angle. Which line has that job?
quiz.explanation: The mainsheet controls the boom and mainsail angle; the halyard hoists the sail.

quiz.prompt: Can the visual winch model assess safe handling of a loaded rope?
options: No; physical line handling needs supervised practice
quiz.explanation: The rendered hardware provides orientation, not a simulation of hand placement, friction, or line loads.

sail-03.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-04.title: Read the instruments
concepts: Heading is the direction the bow points, measured clockwise from north: 000° north, 090° east, 180° south, 270° west. Speed is shown in knots; one knot is one nautical mile per hour.

The wind display identifies the direction the wind comes from. The on-deck wind dial is relative to the bow, while the HUD compass is north-referenced. Depth is the simulator’s water-depth estimate, not clearance below the keel.

In real navigation, course over ground and speed over ground can differ from heading and speed through water because of current and leeway. This simulation estimates both effects; compare heading and water speed with course and speed over ground in Boat systems.
observe: Open Helm or Cockpit and compare the chartplotter and speed display with the HUD.
Open the chart and find the yacht symbol and north arrow.
sail-04.mistake: Reading depth as guaranteed clearance or treating heading as a guaranteed ground track.

quiz.prompt: Which heading points east?
quiz.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north; east is 090°.

quiz.prompt: At 6 knots, how far would you travel in 30 minutes without current?
quiz.explanation: Distance = speed × time. Six nautical miles per hour for half an hour is three nautical miles.

sail-04.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You can now locate the displays. Check instruments regularly while maintaining an outside lookout.

sail-05.title: Where the wind comes from
concepts: A northwesterly wind comes from the northwest and blows toward the southeast. Windward is toward the source of the wind; leeward is away from it.

Here true wind is air motion relative to fixed ground. Apparent wind is relative to the moving yacht; some real instruments use a water reference for true wind, so check their convention. Your motion changes the wind experienced aboard: apparent wind. Our empirical sail-force model uses apparent wind; it is not a validated aerodynamic prediction.
The no-go zone is the sector too close to the wind for the sails to drive the boat. Its limit varies with boat and conditions; this simulator uses 38° on either side.
observe: With wind from 315°, compare headings 315°, 045°, and 135° on the compass.
The 045° heading puts the wind approximately across the side.
sail-05.mistake: Interpreting the arrow as where the wind is going rather than where it comes from.

quiz.prompt: A wind from 315° comes from which direction?
quiz.explanation: 315° is northwest. Wind direction is conventionally named for its source.

quiz.prompt: Why can a yacht not make useful progress aimed directly into the wind?
options: The sails cannot generate effective driving force in that direction
quiz.explanation: You must sail outside the no-go zone and tack to make progress upwind.

sail-05.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-06.title: Raise the sails
concepts: In practice, prepare halyards and sheets, check for fouled lines, and ensure sea room before hoisting. A mainsail is commonly hoisted with the boat pointing into the wind and the sheet eased so it does not fill unexpectedly.

The Raise sails shortcut moves both sails; Boat systems provides separate main and headsail hoist controls. These controls do not assess the real sequence of topping lift, clutches, sail slides, or furling-line handling.
Once set, bear away far enough to fill the sails. A raised sail alone does not guarantee boat speed.
observe: Start the exercise facing into the wind with sails lowered.
Raise the sails; then turn to a sailable course in later exercises.
sail-06.mistake: Assuming raised sails always propel the boat, or hoisting without first checking the lines and boom area.

quiz.prompt: Before a real mainsail hoist, what should be checked?
options: Clear lines, sea room, crew, and an unloaded sail
Whether the boat is at top speed
quiz.explanation: Preparation prevents jams and unexpected sail loading.

quiz.prompt: Does the Raise sails control teach the full real hoisting procedure?
options: No; it is a simplified combined control
Yes; there are no additional steps
Only when the wind exceeds 20 knots
quiz.explanation: You still need supervised practice with halyards, clutches, sail slides, and the vessel’s equipment.

sail-06.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You set the sails in the model. The next exercise starts on a reach where they can produce drive.

sail-07.title: Feel the boat accelerate
concepts: A beam reach puts the wind approximately at right angles to the yacht. It is a useful starting point because the sails can drive the boat without pointing close to the no-go zone.
The yacht accelerates gradually. Watch speed build before applying a large helm angle: steering authority increases with water flow over the rudder.
Start with small adjustments. Centering the helm stops the turn; it does not automatically restore your previous heading.
observe: Begin on 045° with a northwesterly wind, sails set, and anchor up.
Select Set sail and watch speed increase.
sail-07.mistake: Applying full helm while stationary and expecting the yacht to pivot instantly.

quiz.prompt: When does this rudder gain steering authority?
options: As water flow and boat speed increase
quiz.explanation: A yacht normally needs water flow over the rudder to respond.

quiz.prompt: After centering the helm, what happens?
options: The yacht returns automatically to north
The turn reduces and the yacht tends to maintain its new heading
quiz.explanation: The helm controls turning, not a selected compass heading.

sail-07.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: The sail force accelerated the boat; the rudder became useful as speed built.

sail-08.title: Hold a steady course
concepts: Steering a course is a cycle: choose a distant reference, compare the compass, make a small correction, then center the helm before overshooting.
Keep a lookout beyond the instruments. A course that is accurately steered can still lead into danger.
Hold 045° within 5° for ten continuous seconds, with speed above 2 knots. The timer restarts when you leave the tolerance.
observe: Use short port or starboard inputs, then select Center.
Watch heading settle rather than keeping the helm over.
sail-08.mistake: Holding a large correction too long and oscillating from one side of the target to the other.

quiz.prompt: You are approaching your intended heading. What usually helps avoid overshoot?
options: Center the helm in good time
quiz.explanation: The boat has rotational response; reducing the correction early helps the turn settle.

quiz.prompt: Which is a complete steering routine?
options: Look away until the boat drifts
Look out, check heading, make a small correction, reassess
quiz.explanation: Steering and lookout must happen together.

sail-08.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 045° ±5°, above 2 knots, for 10 seconds
steps.hint: Port brings 060° down toward 045°. Center before you reach the target.

practice.debrief: A steady course requires small corrections and anticipation, not continuous large helm input.

sail-09.title: Find a beam reach
concepts: Point of sail describes your heading relative to the wind, not relative to north. On a beam reach the wind is about 90° off the bow.
The boat can be on a beam reach on either tack. With wind from 315°, headings near 045° and 225° are beam reaches.
Steer until the true wind angle is between 80° and 105° and maintain useful speed.
observe: Compare the bow marker with the wind direction.
Notice that two different compass headings can give the same point of sail.
sail-09.mistake: Memorizing a compass heading as a point of sail when the wind direction may change.

quiz.prompt: What defines a beam reach?
quiz.explanation: Points of sail are relative to the wind.

quiz.prompt: If the wind shifts, can an unchanged heading produce a different point of sail?
quiz.explanation: A wind shift changes the angle between the bow and the wind.

sail-09.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a beam reach above 2 knots for 8 seconds

practice.debrief: You selected a course using the wind relationship, rather than the compass alone.

sail-10.title: Sail close hauled
concepts: Close hauled means sailing near the upwind limit with the sails relatively close to the centerline. Do not point so high that the sails luff and speed disappears.
In this simplified model, a true wind angle of 45°–58° is a useful close-hauled exercise. Real yachts need assessment of apparent wind, sail shape, telltales, sea state, and leeway.
As you head up, trim in gradually. Watch whether speed remains healthy instead of chasing the smallest possible wind angle.
observe: Start on a reach and steer nearer to the wind.
Trim inward as the wind angle decreases.
sail-10.mistake: Pinching: pointing too close to the wind and losing the speed that makes the boat and rudder work.

quiz.prompt: What is pinching?
options: Sailing too close to the wind and losing useful drive
Sailing with too much anchor chain
quiz.explanation: A slightly lower course may produce better upwind progress because it preserves speed.

quiz.prompt: Relative to a beam reach, a close-hauled mainsail is generally…
quiz.explanation: As you sail closer to the wind, the sail angle normally comes inward.

sail-10.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 45°–58° off the wind above 2 knots

practice.debrief: You balanced pointing with boat speed. The simulator estimates leeway but does not assess reading physical telltales.

sail-11.title: Bear away to a broad reach
concepts: Bearing away turns the bow away from the wind. The wind angle increases and the sails generally need easing.
On a broad reach the wind comes from aft of the beam. As you approach dead downwind, watch for an unintended gybe when the wind crosses the stern.
Find an angle of 120°–150°, ease the mainsheet, and keep the helm controlled.
observe: Increase your angle to the wind, then ease the sheet.
Keep a margin from dead downwind while learning.
sail-11.mistake: Leaving the mainsheet tight after bearing away or losing track of which side the boom will move to.

quiz.prompt: What happens to wind angle when you bear away?
quiz.explanation: The bow moves farther away from the source of the wind.

quiz.prompt: What maneuver becomes a concern near dead downwind?
quiz.explanation: A small heading or wind change can take the wind across the stern and move the boom.

sail-11.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a broad reach, 120°–150° off the wind

practice.debrief: You increased the wind angle and kept clear of an accidental stern crossing.

sail-12.title: Trim with feedback
concepts: Trim means adjusting the sail to the airflow. A mainsheet pulled in too far can stall the sail; too far out can leave it luffing. Real trimming depends on telltales, sail shape, and feel.
Here the suggested mainsheet angle is a teaching aid calculated from apparent wind angle. Match it, then observe boat speed. It is a model-specific guide, not a universal sail-trim formula.
The trim assessment needs an angle within 6° of the model target and boat speed above 2 knots for ten seconds.
observe: Leave the helm centered and change only the sheet.
Wait for speed to respond instead of making constant large changes.
sail-12.mistake: Changing heading and sheet simultaneously so you cannot tell which adjustment improved the boat.

quiz.prompt: For a useful trim comparison, which technique helps?
options: Hold a steady course and adjust one thing at a time
quiz.explanation: A stable course makes the effects of sheet changes easier to observe.

quiz.prompt: Is the suggested angle a valid rule for all real yachts?
options: No; it belongs to this simplified model
quiz.explanation: Real trim requires observation of the particular sail, boat, and conditions.

sail-12.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold efficient trim and speed for 10 seconds

practice.debrief: You used a controlled adjustment and allowed time for the speed response.

sail-13.title: Head up and bear away
concepts: Heading up turns toward the source of the wind; bearing away turns away from it. Port and starboard name turn direction relative to the boat, not whether you are heading up.
On one tack, a port turn may head up; on the opposite tack it may bear away. Always reason from the current wind direction.
First sail at 50° off the wind, then at 110°. Settle each course before making the next change.
observe: Notice whether the wind angle grows or shrinks with each helm input.
Center the helm at each target, and adjust trim to the new point of sail.

quiz.prompt: Is a port turn always a turn toward the wind?
options: No; it depends on the tack and wind direction
quiz.explanation: The same helm direction changes the wind relationship differently on opposite tacks.

quiz.prompt: What should follow a substantial course change?
quiz.explanation: The new heading changes airflow and the situation around the boat.

sail-13.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You changed your relationship to the wind in both directions and stabilized between turns.

sail-14.title: Make a controlled tack
concepts: A tack takes the bow through the wind, changing which side receives the wind. Check for traffic and sea room, prepare the crew and sheets, then make the turn with sufficient boat speed.
Expect a short loss of drive through the no-go zone. Keep the turn purposeful, then center the helm on the new close-hauled course and trim.
The simulator shifts the sails automatically. This exercise assesses the bow crossing and recovery of control, not real jib-sheet handling or crew calls.
observe: Start with wind over the starboard side, then turn starboard through 315°.
Continue past the no-go zone, center the helm, and rebuild speed.
sail-14.mistake: Stopping the turn in the no-go zone, or calling a turn across the stern a tack.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the yacht crosses the wind during a tack?
quiz.explanation: A tack takes the bow through the source of the wind; a gybe takes the stern through it.

quiz.prompt: Before the turn, what is needed?
options: Lookout, sea room, preparation, and enough boat speed
All crew standing beneath the boom
quiz.explanation: Preparation and momentum help the boat complete the no-go-zone crossing.

sail-14.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Turn the bow through the wind and recover above 2 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard through 315°, then continue to about 005° and center. Trim for the new course.

practice.debrief: The assessment recorded a bow crossing, a new tack, and recovered speed. Sheet transfer remains an on-water skill.

sail-15.title: Make a planned gybe
concepts: A gybe takes the stern through the wind. The boom can cross the cockpit forcefully, so check the area, warn the crew, and control the mainsheet according to your instructor’s procedure.
Approach deliberately on a broad reach and make a small controlled stern crossing. Avoid a large uncontrolled boom swing or an unnecessary turn into a reach on the other side.
Our boom is animated but does not simulate impact forces or crew injury. The assessment recognizes a stern crossing and a stable new broad reach.
observe: Start at 160° with wind from 315°. Turn port toward and through 135°.
Settle near 110° and keep the wind well aft of the beam.
sail-15.mistake: Treating a gybe like an unannounced sharp turn with the mainsheet fully loose.

quiz.prompt: What is the principal gybe hazard for the crew?
options: The boom and mainsheet crossing the cockpit
quiz.explanation: Control the boom and keep people clear of its path.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a gybe from a tack?
options: The stern passes through the wind
The boat must use an engine
quiz.explanation: The wind crosses the stern during a gybe and the bow during a tack.

sail-15.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Cross the wind with the stern and settle on the new tack
steps.hint: Turn port through 135° and settle near 110°. Center the helm.

practice.debrief: You made the correct stern crossing. Real mainsheet control must be learned with supervision.

sail-16.title: Recover from loss of drive
concepts: In irons means stopped or nearly stopped pointing into the wind. The sails luff and the rudder loses authority as speed falls.
Avoid the situation by keeping momentum during a tack and not pinching. This exercise begins with residual forward motion: bear away promptly and trim to restore drive.

A completely stopped real yacht may require a backed sail, engine assistance, or a vessel-specific recovery method. Backing sails is not modeled. The engine is available in free sailing, but this residual-way exercise requires neutral; restart if all steerage is lost.
observe: Use the remaining way to turn away from 315°.
Do not wait until speed reaches zero before correcting.
sail-16.mistake: Expecting the rudder to rotate a fully stationary yacht without water flow.

quiz.prompt: Why should you act before all speed is lost?
options: Residual water flow gives steering authority
quiz.explanation: Use the remaining steerage to get outside the no-go zone.

quiz.prompt: Does this exercise teach all methods of recovering a fully stopped real yacht?
options: No; this exercise assesses residual-way recovery under sail
quiz.explanation: The exercise covers recovery with residual way; real recovery depends on the vessel and situation.

sail-16.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Exit the no-go zone and rebuild speed above 2 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard toward 010° or beyond before the remaining way disappears.

practice.debrief: You used residual momentum. A stopped-boat recovery is a separate practical skill.

sail-17.title: True and apparent wind
concepts: A moving yacht experiences apparent wind: the air motion relative to the boat. Even on a calm day, moving forward produces airflow from ahead.
As boat speed increases, apparent wind generally shifts forward relative to the true wind. Downwind, motion in the same direction as the wind can reduce the apparent wind speed.

Compare true wind on the wind dial with apparent wind in Boat systems. Sail force and suggested sheet angles use apparent wind; this empirical model is not a substitute for reading telltales and sail shape.
observe: Imagine riding a bicycle in still air: you feel wind from ahead.
Compare the apparent wind display as speed increases on a steady course.
sail-17.mistake: Assuming true and apparent wind have identical direction and speed while the yacht is moving.

quiz.prompt: What wind does a moving sail actually experience?
quiz.explanation: Sails interact with airflow relative to the moving yacht.

quiz.prompt: What does this prototype use for its sail-force calculation?
options: An empirical model using apparent wind
quiz.explanation: Apparent wind reflects vessel motion. The empirical force model still omits many real aerodynamic details.

sail-17.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-18.title: Reef before you need to
concepts: Reefing reduces sail area to improve control as wind increases. A decision to reef should consider forecast, gusts, sea state, crew ability, and the boat’s behavior, not a universal wind-speed rule.
Excessive heel, heavy helm, and difficulty maintaining control are reasons to reassess sail area early. Delaying can make the work harder when conditions deteriorate.
The Reef control reduces mainsail height and modeled drive. It does not teach reefing-line, tack-cringle, or halyard procedures.
observe: Observe heel and speed in the exercise’s 22-knot breeze.
Select Reef, keep the boat on a reach, and compare its response.
sail-18.mistake: Waiting until the crew are overloaded or using a fixed wind threshold without considering the boat.

quiz.prompt: What is a sound reason to reef early?
options: Increasing difficulty keeping the yacht controlled
Every yacht always reefs at exactly 20 knots
quiz.explanation: Reefing is a control decision based on boat, crew, and conditions.

quiz.prompt: Which real skill is not assessed by the Reef button?
options: Managing halyards and reefing lines under load
quiz.explanation: The single control abstracts several important physical tasks.

sail-18.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Set a reef and maintain steerage for 10 seconds

practice.debrief: You reduced sail area and retained control. Real reefing needs a practiced crew procedure.

sail-19.title: Reduce power deliberately
concepts: Reducing driving force slows the boat, but momentum remains. Leave sea room and avoid treating a sailing yacht like a car with immediate brakes.
You can spill some drive by easing the mainsheet. Lowering sails removes modeled sail power; the yacht then coasts and loses steerage as it slows.
For this exercise, reduce sail power, lower the sails, and wait until speed is below 1 knot. The anchor is not a substitute for a planned speed reduction.
observe: Compare the speed before and after lowering sails.
Notice the delay and the reduction in rudder authority.
sail-19.mistake: Dropping an anchor at speed as a routine way to stop.

quiz.prompt: What remains after you lower the sails?
quiz.explanation: The boat continues to move until drag reduces its speed.

quiz.prompt: Why leave room when slowing down?
options: Stopping distance and declining steerage need to be anticipated
The compass becomes unreliable at low speed
quiz.explanation: Plan your speed reduction early enough to remain in control.

sail-19.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You allowed momentum to decay instead of expecting an immediate stop.

sail-20.title: Choose a weather limit
concepts: Read a marine forecast for the whole intended trip and a margin beyond it. Consider mean wind, gusts, direction changes, sea state, visibility, temperature, tides, and local effects.
Wind against current can steepen waves. Offshore wind can make returning difficult; an exposed lee shore can leave little room to recover from a failure.

Set a go/no-go decision and escape options before departure. The simulation has adjustable steady wind but no gust fronts, breaking-wave hazards, weather forecasting, or changing tidal streams; adjustable current is a steady approximation.
observe: For a novice crew, decide what change would make you shorten or cancel a trip.
Name a sheltered alternative and a return deadline.
sail-20.mistake: Treating a low average wind speed as proof that the entire trip will be safe.

quiz.prompt: The average wind is manageable but the forecast includes strong gusts and worsening visibility. What is appropriate?
options: Depart because only average speed matters
Reassess the trip against crew ability and safe alternatives
quiz.explanation: The entire forecast and its trend matter, not one number.

quiz.prompt: Can this simulation assess handling breaking seas or wind-against-tide conditions?
quiz.explanation: Those environmental dynamics are not implemented and require separate instruction.

sail-20.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-21.title: Read a practice chart
concepts: A chart is a planning tool, not a picture to follow blindly. Check scale, orientation, depth information, hazards, marks, and the source and currency of the chart.
Our fictional chart shows islands, your yacht, and amber course buoys. These amber marks are training targets; they are not a representation of the complete IALA buoyage system.
Before a real passage, learn chart symbols, chart datum, local buoyage, tidal heights, and under-keel clearance. None should be inferred from this simplified map.
observe: Open the chart. Locate north, your position, and the next mark.
Identify land you must keep clear of along the intended route.
sail-21.mistake: Assuming a screen showing your position is a complete and current navigational chart.

quiz.prompt: What do the three amber buoys in this app represent?
options: Guaranteed safe-water marks on a real chart
quiz.explanation: Their purpose is exercise navigation, not teaching every real-world mark.

quiz.prompt: Which should a real chart check include?
options: Scale, source, currency, depths, hazards, and local conventions
quiz.explanation: Charts need interpretation and context to support safe navigation.

sail-21.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-22.title: Steer toward a waypoint
concepts: A bearing is the direction from your position to a target. Decide whether the direct track is safe and sailable before following it.
A direct bearing may point into the no-go zone or cross land. In those cases, plan a different route rather than forcing the bow toward the target.
The exercise starts south of buoy 1. Use the chart, steer toward the mark, and pass within 35 metres while keeping speed controlled.
observe: Open the chart before changing course.
Aim toward buoy 1, then check progress and depth regularly.
sail-22.mistake: Fixating on the target and ignoring land, traffic, or the wind angle.

quiz.prompt: Your waypoint lies directly upwind. What is required?
options: Plan a sailable route using tacks
Hold the bow in the no-go zone indefinitely
Increase the compass reading until the wind changes
quiz.explanation: You may need multiple legs to make progress toward an upwind destination.

quiz.prompt: Is the direct bearing always a safe course?
options: Only if the waypoint is visible
No; check hazards, depth, wind, and traffic
quiz.explanation: A bearing describes direction, not safety.

sail-22.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Open the chart to plan the approach
Reach buoy 1 with at least 3 m depth

practice.debrief: You related chart position to the world and monitored a real approach in the simulation.

sail-23.title: Estimate distance and time
concepts: For a first estimate, distance equals speed multiplied by time. At 4 knots, a 3-nautical-mile leg takes 45 minutes if speed remains constant and there is no current.
Dead reckoning advances an earlier position using course, speed, and time. Real estimates also account for current, leeway, and uncertainty; a fix from observations checks the estimate.
Record assumptions and update the estimate as conditions change. Do not confuse a precise-looking number with an accurate prediction.
observe: Compute the time for 3 nautical miles at 4 knots before checking the answer.
Describe one reason the actual arrival time might differ.
sail-23.mistake: Mixing minutes and hours or ignoring current and changing boat speed.

quiz.prompt: At 4 knots, how long is a 3-nautical-mile leg without current?
quiz.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 hours = 0.75 hour = 45 minutes.

quiz.prompt: What checks an estimated position?
options: Assuming the log cannot be wrong
An independent position observation or fix
quiz.explanation: An estimate needs verification and an allowance for uncertainty.

sail-23.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-24.title: Sail a short passage
concepts: Break a route into manageable legs with clear targets, hazards, and a plan for the next turn. Keep a lookout before altering course at a mark.
This exercise runs from south of buoy 1 to buoy 1, then buoy 2. The wind makes both direct legs sailable, but you still need to turn and retrim.
Keep at least 3 metres of modeled water depth. Grounding invalidates the attempt and requires a restart; passing the marks alone is not sufficient.
observe: Study both legs before setting off.
At buoy 1, look toward buoy 2 and prepare the course change.
sail-24.mistake: Reaching a waypoint without planning what happens immediately afterward.

quiz.prompt: When should the next leg be considered?
options: Only after leaving the chart behind
Before arriving at the turning point
Never; the yacht follows marks automatically
quiz.explanation: Anticipation leaves time for lookout, crew preparation, and safe course changes.

quiz.prompt: You passed the marks but ran aground. Was the passage successful?
options: No; avoiding hazards is part of the task
Yes, if the speed was high
quiz.explanation: A completed route is not a safe route if essential margins were lost.

sail-24.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You planned and sailed two connected legs. Tides, traffic, and real pilotage require additional training.

sail-25.title: Keep an effective lookout
concepts: A proper lookout uses sight, hearing, and appropriate available means. Scan ahead, astern, and to both sides; the sails and structures can hide other craft.
A vessel staying on a nearly constant bearing while getting closer is a warning of collision risk. Reassess early rather than waiting for certainty at close range.
Electronic aids support the lookout; they do not replace it. This world has static moored yachts and does not assess realistic traffic detection.
observe: Use the camera to scan the side hidden by the headsail.
Explain how you would share lookout duties with a real crew.
sail-25.mistake: Looking only ahead or only at the chartplotter.

quiz.prompt: A nearby vessel stays at a nearly constant bearing while the distance closes. What might that indicate?
options: No risk because it is not changing direction on the window
A guarantee that it will pass astern
quiz.explanation: Constant bearing with decreasing range is a classic warning; act early based on the full situation.

quiz.prompt: Can a chartplotter replace sight and hearing?
quiz.explanation: Use all appropriate available means and keep an outside lookout.

sail-25.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-26.title: Reason through encounters
concepts: For two sailing vessels in the basic crossing cases: different tacks generally means the port-tack vessel keeps clear of the starboard-tack vessel; on the same tack, the windward vessel generally keeps clear of the leeward vessel.

An overtaking vessel keeps clear. Other vessel responsibilities, narrow channels, traffic schemes, restricted visibility, and local rules can change the analysis. Do not reduce the rules to “sail always wins.”
A stand-on vessel still has responsibilities and must act when needed to avoid collision. Learn the full applicable collision regulations and local requirements before sailing.
observe: Identify the windward side of each vessel before deciding its tack.
State the assumptions before applying a simplified crossing rule.
sail-26.mistake: Treating stand-on status as permission to ignore developing collision risk.

quiz.prompt: In a basic two-sailing-vessel encounter on different tacks, which normally keeps clear?
quiz.explanation: Under the basic sailing-vessel rule, port tack keeps clear of starboard tack, subject to the full situation and other applicable rules.

quiz.prompt: Does a stand-on vessel have no further responsibility?
options: No; it must continue monitoring and act as required to avoid collision
Yes; it can close its eyes
Yes; the other vessel accepts all responsibility
quiz.explanation: Collision avoidance is an ongoing duty. The complete rules specify stand-on actions and responsibilities.

sail-26.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-27.title: Lights, marks, and signals
concepts: Navigation lights and day shapes communicate a vessel’s type and activity, not just its direction. Red and green sidelights help identify which aspect you are seeing.

In the international maneuvering-signal context, one short blast means altering course to starboard, two to port, and three operating astern propulsion. Restricted-visibility signals are a different system; local or inland rules may differ.

This introductory lesson does not cover the full recognition syllabus. Before night or restricted-visibility operation, study and practice the complete applicable lights, shapes, and sound-signal rules.
observe: Identify the red port light and green starboard light on the yacht.
Distinguish an action signal from a signal used in restricted visibility.
sail-27.mistake: Assuming one memorized signal applies in every jurisdiction and situation.

quiz.prompt: Which side normally carries the red sidelight?
quiz.explanation: The port sidelight is red; starboard is green.

quiz.prompt: In the stated international maneuvering-signal context, two short blasts indicate…
quiz.explanation: Two short blasts mean altering course to port in that context; do not generalize without checking the applicable rules.

sail-27.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-28.title: Make a passage decision
concepts: A passage plan includes the crew, forecast, route, hazards, tidal constraints, daylight, safe havens, communications, and a latest turn-back time.
Good seamanship includes changing or abandoning the plan when its assumptions fail. Do not let a fixed arrival promise outweigh safety margins.
Scenario: you have a novice crew, fading daylight, a forecast wind increase, and an exposed destination. A nearby sheltered alternative is available.
observe: Name the factors that make the original destination less suitable.
Choose a conservative alternative and tell the crew why.
sail-28.mistake: Continuing because the destination was promised before conditions changed.

quiz.prompt: For the stated scenario, which is the sounder decision?
options: Press on to preserve the schedule
Ask the least experienced crew member to decide alone
Reassess and favor the sheltered alternative or an early return
quiz.explanation: Rising exposure and shrinking margins support a conservative change of plan.

quiz.prompt: Which makes an abort plan useful?
options: Clear decision points and viable alternatives
Leaving every decision until the last minute
A promise never to change course
quiz.explanation: Specific triggers and alternatives help avoid rushed decisions under pressure.

sail-28.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-29.title: Plan a docking approach
concepts: Docking combines wind, current, propeller effects, boat momentum, and crew coordination. Prepare fenders and lines, assign roles, choose an approach, and keep an escape route.
Approach at the lowest speed that preserves the control you need. Never use a person’s body to stop the boat or put hands or feet between the yacht and dock.

Boat systems includes ahead and reverse thrust, and the model estimates current. Prop walk, spring-line forces, and dock contact are not modeled. Docking is taught here as planning and decision-making; touching the visual dock is not an assessed docking skill.
observe: Describe your approach, crew jobs, and go-around plan before moving.
Explain why wind and current change a safe approach.
sail-29.mistake: Relying on crew to jump ashore or physically catch the yacht.

quiz.prompt: If the approach becomes unstable, what should the preplanned option be?
options: Ask someone to fend off with a foot
Abort and make a controlled new approach if safe
Add speed to get it over with
quiz.explanation: An escape plan is part of preparation; avoid trapping the boat or crew in an unrecoverable maneuver.

quiz.prompt: Can arriving beside the rendered pontoon prove docking competence here?
options: No; dock contact, spring lines, and crew tasks are not assessed
Yes, if the boat looks aligned
quiz.explanation: A visual result without the relevant dynamics is not a valid skill assessment.

sail-29.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-30.title: Choose an anchorage
concepts: Choose shelter, suitable holding ground, adequate depth throughout the tidal range, and room to swing without reaching hazards or neighboring vessels.
Scope compares the rode deployed with the vertical distance from bow roller to seabed. Required scope depends on rode, anchor, conditions, boat, and guidance; no single ratio guarantees holding.

Example for arithmetic only: at 5 m water depth and a roller 1 m above water, an assumed 5:1 ratio gives 30 m of rode. This calculation is not a deployment prescription. Add tidal changes and assess swing room.
observe: Sketch the expected swing circle and nearby hazards.
Include roller height in the example’s vertical distance.
sail-30.mistake: Multiplying charted depth alone or assuming an anchor always holds once it touches bottom.

quiz.prompt: Under the stated example assumptions, how much rode corresponds to 5:1?
quiz.explanation: The vertical distance is 5 + 1 = 6 m. Five times 6 m is 30 m, before other real-world considerations.

quiz.prompt: What must an anchorage plan consider beyond depth?
options: Only the distance to a café
Shelter, holding ground, tide, swing room, and hazards
quiz.explanation: Depth alone does not establish a suitable or safe anchorage.

sail-30.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-31.title: Stop, then anchor
concepts: A real anchoring approach is controlled and slow. The crew lowers the anchor and deploys rode deliberately, then checks that it has set and continues monitoring position.

The rode target is a command, not the length in the water. Check actual paid-out rode in Systems. Lowering runs at a modeled 24 metres per minute and retrieval at 15 metres per minute; these are illustrative powered rates.

Lower sails and coast below 0.8 knots with the anchor stowed. Then set a 45 m rode target and run the windlass. It pays out gradually and stops at the target. Use Stop windlass to halt it and Run to target to continue. Wait for 45 m actually paid out, the windlass stopped, and ground speed below 0.2 knots. Deploying early invalidates the attempt.

The 45 m target belongs to this prepared shallow-water exercise. Plan a real anchorage from its depth, tide, shelter, holding ground, and swing room. The model does not validate anchor setting in a particular seabed or represent full rode catenary.
observe: Reduce sail power well before the intended stopping point.
Wait for speed to fall before using the anchor control.
sail-31.mistake: Deploying the anchor at speed instead of completing a controlled approach.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct sequence in this exercise?
options: Anchor at full speed, then lower sails
Lower sails, slow with anchor up, then anchor
quiz.explanation: The exercise checks anticipation and sequencing, not the anchor’s holding ability.

quiz.prompt: Does the stopped position demonstrate that a real anchor is properly set?
options: No; modeled holding cannot prove real anchor setting
quiz.explanation: Real anchoring requires checks of holding and ongoing monitoring.

sail-31.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Lower sails and coast below 0.8 knots, anchor up
Pay out 45 m, stop the windlass, and settle below 0.2 knots

practice.debrief: You practiced a controlled stop and the correct simplified sequence. Real anchor setting is not assessed.

sail-32.title: Prepare to leave
concepts: Before departure, recheck the surrounding area, intended route, conditions, and crew readiness. Make sure lines and equipment are secure and everyone knows what happens next.

This exercise starts with 45 m of rode already paid out and the bow above the anchor. Select Weigh anchor and watch actual rode length reduce. The anchor remains deployed during retrieval. Wait until it is fully stowed before raising sails, then establish a steady reach.

If the rode becomes taut while the boat is away from the anchor, retrieval pauses. In free sailing, move slowly toward the anchor to slacken the rode, then continue recovery. The windlass must not be used to tow the boat toward the anchor.

In a real harbor, weigh-anchor and sail-hoisting plans depend on shelter, space, traffic, wind, engine availability, and the vessel. The simulator’s convenient setup is not a universal departure procedure.
observe: Confirm the wind and your intended course before releasing the hold.
Restore sail power, gain steerage, and make a controlled departure.
sail-32.mistake: Releasing the boat before having a clear plan and adequate room.

quiz.prompt: What belongs before releasing the boat?
options: Crew briefing, lookout, and a clear plan
Looking at the route only after leaving
quiz.explanation: Preparation should precede the point at which the vessel is free to move.

quiz.prompt: Is this open-water sail departure a method for every real anchorage?
options: No; plan for the specific boat, space, and conditions
Only if a chartplotter is fitted
quiz.explanation: The exercise omits many constraints of actual anchorages and harbors.

sail-32.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

practice.debrief: You restored movement deliberately and established control in a prepared practice area.

sail-33.title: Person overboard priorities
concepts: Raise the alarm, maintain continuous visual contact, point to the person, and deploy appropriate flotation and marking equipment. Assign roles and call for help as the situation requires.

A successful recovery includes getting the yacht safely back to the casualty, stopping in a suitable position, avoiding propeller injury, and lifting the person aboard. The precise maneuver depends on vessel, sail plan, conditions, and training.

There is no person-overboard dynamics or recovery model here. This lesson checks priorities only. Practice a vessel-specific maneuver and recovery system with an instructor, using a training object rather than putting a person at risk.
observe: Assign a dedicated pointer who does not lose sight of the casualty.
Explain why returning alongside is only one part of recovery.
sail-33.mistake: Everyone looking at the controls while nobody keeps the casualty in sight.

quiz.prompt: What is an immediate priority after the alarm?
options: Keep visual contact and deploy appropriate flotation/marking aids
Wait to see whether the person swims back
quiz.explanation: Tracking and supporting the casualty are urgent while the crew organizes the recovery and help.

quiz.prompt: Does reaching the casualty complete the task?
options: No; safe stopping, lifting aboard, and aftercare also matter
quiz.explanation: Recovery includes the difficult physical steps and casualty care, not just navigation.

sail-33.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-34.title: Distress and urgent action
concepts: Distress means grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Know the vessel’s communications equipment, local procedures, and how to give identity, position, nature of the emergency, and assistance needed.

For an immediate life-threatening situation, use the appropriate distress facilities, such as DSC distress and a MAYDAY call on VHF channel 16 where applicable and available. Learn the equipment before departure and never transmit a real distress alert for practice.

After a grounding, flooding, or fire, protect people, assess the situation, call for help as needed, and follow vessel-specific emergency procedures. Blindly applying power after grounding may worsen damage.
observe: Rehearse the information you would provide without transmitting.
Locate the simulated position and explain what a real rescue service needs.
sail-34.mistake: Giving a long story but omitting position, identity, or the kind of help needed.

quiz.prompt: Which information is central to a distress message?
options: Identity, position, danger, and assistance needed
quiz.explanation: Clear essential information helps rescuers locate the vessel and prioritize a response.

quiz.prompt: How should you practice an emergency radio message?
options: Make a real distress transmission for realism
Rehearse without transmitting, or use an authorized training setting
quiz.explanation: False distress alerts can divert real emergency resources.

sail-34.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-35.title: Your assessed first passage
concepts: Combine the course skills without rushing: establish a steady course, trim effectively, change tack through the bow, recover control, and slow to a planned stop.
The simulator gives measured targets but no automatic steering. Each stage must be completed in order. Grounding or using the anchor before the final stopping stage invalidates the attempt.

The final stage uses a prepared deep-water anchorage and a 180 m rode target. Wait for all 180 m to be paid out, the windlass to stop, and ground speed to fall below 0.2 knots. Allow about 15 minutes for the complete exercise. This target is specific to these training conditions.
Passing demonstrates the selected modeled tasks in steady wind and open water. It does not establish real-world navigation, docking, emergency recovery, or skipper competence.
observe: Brief yourself on the sequence before selecting Begin practice.
Use the checklist and retain lookout while monitoring the instruments.
sail-35.mistake: Treating isolated skills as independent of lookout, sea room, and the next step.

quiz.prompt: Which result counts as a successful simulated passage?
options: Completing the stages in order while keeping the safety margins
quiz.explanation: The assessment combines controlled performance, sequence, and maintained margins.

quiz.prompt: If a task is invalidated, what is the right response?
options: Restart, understand the cause, and practice again
Ignore the warning and claim a pass
Change the weather until the result is accepted
quiz.explanation: Reviewing the cause is part of learning; invalid attempts do not earn a pass.

sail-35.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Tack through the bow and recover speed
steps.hint: From 045°, turn port through 315° and settle near 265°.

steps.label: Lower sails and coast below 0.8 knots
Pay out 180 m, stop the windlass, and settle below 0.2 knots

practice.debrief: You linked steering, trimming, tacking, and stopping. Review any hints used and repeat with less assistance.

sail-36.title: From simulation to the sea
concepts: Review the difference between explaining a task, performing it in this model, and performing it aboard a real yacht. Your course record separates theory checks from simulated practice and records the use of hints.

The next step is supervised on-water training: preparation and equipment checks; knots and line handling; hoisting, trimming, reefing, tacking and gybing with crew; engine handling and docking; real anchoring; lookout and navigation; and person-overboard recovery.

Choose an instructor and conditions appropriate to your experience. Bring your course record, explain the simulator’s limitations, and ask for an individual practical assessment. Course completion here is a learning milestone, not a license or safety certification.
observe: Review your record and identify the exercises where you used hints or repeated attempts.
Write down three real-world skills that still need supervised practice.
sail-36.mistake: Treating a completion badge as evidence that every real boat and condition can be handled safely.

quiz.prompt: What should follow successful completion?
options: Supervised on-water training and practical assessment
Immediate solo sailing in unfamiliar conditions
Assuming docking and rescue were already mastered
quiz.explanation: The course supports preparation; it does not replace real experience and instruction.

quiz.prompt: Which important skills remain unassessed by this simulator?
options: Loaded line handling, engine docking, and casualty recovery
quiz.explanation: Those skills require forces, equipment, coordination, and conditions that this version does not model.

sail-36.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-37.title: Plan the route and the escape
concepts: A passage plan connects preparation, route, execution and monitoring. Check current charts and notices, forecast, tide and current, daylight, boat readiness, crew capability, fuel and communications. Mark hazards, safe water, alternatives and points where choices become limited.

Choose decision points before departure. In this fictional exercise, the exposed headland is acceptable only if the agreed weather and daylight margins remain available. A sheltered alternative is available before the headland; after passing it, returning may be difficult.

A route is a proposal to keep checking. Compare actual progress and conditions with the plan. A pre-agreed diversion trigger helps avoid continuing simply because the destination is close. Share the route, crew roles and contingency plan.
observe: Write a primary route, one sheltered alternative and one clear diversion trigger.
Identify the last safe decision point before the exposed section.
sail-37.mistake: Selecting a destination and following its waypoint without checking hazards or preserving an escape option.

quiz.prompt: Before an exposed headland, the forecast worsens beyond your agreed limit. A sheltered alternative remains open. What best follows the plan?
options: Continue because the headland is nearby
Use the sheltered alternative while it remains viable
Increase speed and decide after rounding
quiz.explanation: Act at the planned decision point. Keeping an acceptable alternative avoids committing to conditions beyond the agreed limits.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a contingency usable?
options: A specific trigger, safe alternative and decision point
A promise to reach the destination
A spare waypoint without checking its approach
quiz.explanation: A contingency needs a feasible option and a clear moment to act, checked against conditions and crew capability.

sail-37.transfer: With an instructor, plan a real short passage using current local charts, forecasts and tide information. Walk through the alternatives and the places where turning back becomes difficult.

sail-38.title: Tidal depth and clearance
concepts: Charted depths refer to a stated chart datum. A predicted tidal height can be added only when its datum, location, date and time are compatible with that chart. Water depth is not the same as clearance beneath the keel. Confirm what a real depth instrument measures and its offset.

Fictional static example: charted depth 2.4 m plus tidal height 1.1 m gives water depth 3.5 m. Subtract a 1.8 m draft to get 1.7 m static under-keel clearance. If the exercise requires a 0.8 m allowance, 0.9 m remains above that allowance. This is arithmetic, not permission to cross a shoal.

Real clearance planning also considers the lowest tide during passage, survey and forecast uncertainty, waves, squat, heel and vessel/operator guidance. Do not add tidal height again to an instrument reading that already represents water depth. A favorable single reading cannot establish a safe route.
observe: Label chart datum, tidal height, water depth and draft separately in the example.
List information missing before you could approve a real shallow-water passage.
sail-38.mistake: Treating charted depth or a depth-display number as guaranteed under-keel clearance.

quiz.prompt: For the stated example, what is the static clearance before the 0.8 m allowance?
quiz.explanation: Water depth is 2.4 + 1.1 = 3.5 m. Subtracting the 1.8 m draft leaves 1.7 m.

quiz.prompt: Why does that calculation not approve a real crossing?
options: Datum/time, changing tide, uncertainty and dynamic allowances still need checking
quiz.explanation: A static arithmetic result omits changing conditions and uncertainties. Confirm compatible data and adequate vessel-specific margins.

sail-38.transfer: Practice with a current local chart and tide source under instruction. Confirm chart datum, time zone, tidal station, vessel draft and the actual sounder offset before using any number.

sail-39.title: Current vectors and passage time
concepts: Heading is where the bow points. Course over ground is the direction of movement over the seabed. Speed through water and speed over ground differ because current adds a velocity vector; leeway can add another difference. Current set names the direction it flows toward.

Fictional straight-line example: a yacht makes 5 knots through the water directly along a 12 nautical mile route. A steady 1-knot current directly against the route gives 4 knots over ground, so the leg takes 3 hours. A directly following current gives 6 knots and 2 hours. Ignore acceleration and leeway only for this example.

Cross-current must be combined as a vector, not simply added to or subtracted from speed. It changes ground track and may require a different course to steer. Real passages need time-varying current, wind, tacking, sea conditions and a reserve; recalculate ETA using observed progress.
observe: Compare heading and water speed with course and speed over ground in Boat systems.
Draw ahead, opposing and cross-current arrows before doing arithmetic.
sail-39.mistake: Using water speed for every arrival estimate or subtracting a cross-current as if it flowed directly astern.

quiz.prompt: At 5 knots through water with a directly opposing 1-knot current, how long is the stated 12 nautical mile leg?
quiz.explanation: The example gives 4 knots over ground. Time = 12 nautical miles ÷ 4 knots = 3 hours.

quiz.prompt: What changes when the same current flows across the route?
options: Combine velocity vectors and reassess track/course to steer
Always subtract 1 knot from water speed
Heading and ground track must remain identical
quiz.explanation: A cross-current changes the direction of ground motion. Scalar addition works only for collinear velocities in these simple examples.

sail-39.transfer: Use a navigation instructor and real tidal-stream data to plot a course to steer. Compare planned and observed progress without treating this app’s current as a local forecast.

sail-40.title: Weather: go, wait or divert
concepts: A weather limit belongs to a specific boat, crew, route and set of conditions. Review official marine forecasts and warnings, gusts, wind direction, sea state, visibility, tide/current interaction and safe alternatives. A single wind number does not describe the risk.

Fictional decision: your crew agreed to avoid an exposed leg if gusts increase beyond its practiced capability or visibility removes the pilotage references. Either trigger is now forecast before you can complete the leg. Waiting or choosing an acceptable sheltered route preserves the agreed margin.

Check updates and conditions underway. Wind against current can steepen seas; an onshore wind can increase lee-shore danger. Reduce sail early as appropriate, preserve crew energy and change the plan before options narrow. A reef does not make every forecast acceptable.
observe: State two departure limits and where you would reassess them underway.
Compare the exposed route with its sheltered alternative for wind direction, sea state and visibility.
sail-40.mistake: Treating a universal wind-speed threshold or the ability to reef as proof that a passage is safe.

quiz.prompt: The forecast exceeds your crew’s agreed capability before the exposed leg ends. What is the sound planning response?
options: Reef and assume all risk is removed
Ignore the forecast if the harbor is calm
Wait or choose a checked alternative within the limits
quiz.explanation: The departure decision should preserve the margins agreed for this crew, yacht and route. Harbor conditions do not establish offshore conditions.

quiz.prompt: Why consider current as well as wind?
options: Wind against current can steepen the sea and change the route’s risk
Current affects only the compass display
quiz.explanation: Opposing wind and current can worsen sea conditions. Exposure and the forecast must be considered together.

sail-40.transfer: Discuss a real forecast with an instructor, including local effects and uncertainty. Agree boat- and crew-specific limits and keep reassessing; these examples prescribe no universal safe wind speed.

sail-41.title: Collision risk and limited visibility
concepts: Maintain a lookout by sight, hearing and all appropriate available means. Repeated observations matter: an approaching vessel with little change in compass bearing indicates collision risk. A changing bearing does not always remove risk, especially close by or near a large vessel or tow. If in doubt, treat risk as present.

Safe speed allows effective avoiding action and stopping within the circumstances. Visibility, traffic, maneuverability, wind/sea/current and nearby hazards all matter. Take timely action under the applicable rules and keep checking its effect until the other vessel is past and clear; a single AIS symbol is not a complete lookout.

Under International Rule 19, vessels not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility use a different framework from the in-sight sailing/power encounter rules. Reduce to a safe speed, maintain lookout, use required signals and available equipment correctly. A power-driven vessel must have engines ready for immediate maneuver. Learn the complete applicable rules with an instructor; this exercise selects no universal avoiding turn.
observe: Sketch successive compass bearings and ranges rather than relying on one glimpse.
Identify what information is missing when a vessel is heard or detected electronically but cannot be seen.
sail-41.mistake: Claiming an automatic right of way in fog or assuming that no AIS target means no vessel.

quiz.prompt: A vessel’s range is decreasing while its compass bearing barely changes. What should you conclude?
options: Collision risk exists and needs continuing assessment and timely action
The other vessel will certainly pass astern
quiz.explanation: Little bearing change on approach is a collision-risk indicator. Use appropriate available information and act under the applicable rules.

quiz.prompt: In restricted visibility, another vessel is not in sight. Which statement is sound under International Rule 19?
options: A sailing yacht always has priority over an unseen motor vessel
Apply the restricted-visibility framework, safe speed and proper lookout
Keep speed until visual contact is made
quiz.explanation: The in-sight sailing/power rules cannot simply be applied to an unseen contact. Rule 19 and the general rules require a situation-specific response.

sail-41.transfer: Study the full International and applicable inland/local rules with a qualified instructor. Practice systematic lookout and equipment use aboard; this lesson does not assess real collision avoidance.

sail-42.title: Night pilotage and cross-checks
concepts: Plan a night approach before darkness: identify expected lights and their characteristics, safe water, hazards, clearing bearings, depth expectations, decision points and a safe alternative. Use current charts and publications. A light’s color alone cannot identify it; background lights can confuse the picture.

Cross-check electronic position with independent evidence such as identified lights, bearings, transits and depth trends, allowing for tide and instrument offsets. Two displays using the same GPS source are not independent fixes. Confirm chart scale, datum and updates; a precise-looking symbol can still be wrong.

Fictional approach: the plotter suggests you are on track, but an expected leading-light alignment and the depth trend disagree. Do not continue into shallower or confined water merely to resolve the puzzle. Reduce risk, remain in or return to verified safe water if feasible, cross-check the observations and revise the plan.
observe: List the expected navigation references in their approach order and explain how each will be identified.

sail-42.mistake: Trusting a bright plotter symbol over conflicting observations or treating two screens sharing one sensor as independent confirmation.

quiz.prompt: Two screens share the same GPS source. Do matching positions provide independent confirmation?
options: Yes, because there are two screens
Only when both displays are bright
No; use a genuinely independent observation or source
quiz.explanation: A shared sensor can produce the same error on both screens. Identified visual references and properly interpreted depth can provide other evidence.

quiz.prompt: Plotter position conflicts with the expected light alignment and depth trend before a narrow entrance. What is the prudent response?
options: Maintain speed and trust the plotted line
Reduce risk in verified safe water and resolve the disagreement before committing
quiz.explanation: Conflicting observations reduce confidence. Preserve sea room and cross-check before continuing into a constrained approach.

sail-42.transfer: Rehearse a real pilotage plan with an instructor in daylight before supervised night work. Practice identifying light characteristics and obtaining independent position checks.
